body:
Location and historical setting

The Bagh Caves are situated near Bagh in Dhar district, Madhya Pradesh. They lie on the southern slopes of the Vindhyan region, near the Baghani River.

The caves are rock-cut monuments associated with Buddhist monastic life. Their principal development is generally placed around the 4th–6th centuries CE, broadly overlapping with the flourishing of classical painting at Ajanta.

Bagh originally comprised 9 rock-cut caves. Only 5 of the original caves are generally described as surviving.

These caves were primarily associated with Buddhist monastic residence and religious activities.

Cave 4: The Rang Mahal

The most important cave for painting identification is Cave 4, known as Rang Mahal, meaning the Palace of Colours.

It is especially associated with the remains of the Bagh mural tradition.

The paintings were executed on prepared wall and ceiling surfaces. Their preparation involved a plaster ground and a lime-based surface layer.

The painting tradition at Bagh shares important characteristics with Ajanta, but it developed its own regional expressions.

Bagh Caves = Dhar district, Madhya Pradesh = Buddhist monastic setting = Cave 4, Rang Mahal.

Subjects depicted in Bagh paintings

Although Bagh was a Buddhist religious establishment, its murals were not confined to images of religious worship.

The paintings represent a wide range of subjects, including:

  • Royal and courtly gatherings.
  • Processions and attendants.
  • Dancers and musicians.
  • Human interaction and scenes associated with social life.
  • Subjects connected with the Buddhist cultural environment.

These depictions are valuable because they reveal aspects of the material and social culture of their time.

Painted clothing, bodily gestures and arrangements of people in groups provide evidence of artistic conventions and social activities.

The presence of dancers, musicians and royal subjects should therefore not lead to the conclusion that Bagh was primarily a royal palace or a Hindu temple. Its archaeological context is Buddhist.

Distinctive characteristics of Bagh painting

The Bagh murals are known for their expressive human figures, energetic movement, rhythmic arrangements and lively narrative character.

The figures often communicate actions and emotions through their postures and gestures.

Groups of musicians, dancers and attendants help create the impression of an active social setting.

The painted surfaces and natural pigments show technical continuity with classical Indian mural traditions, especially Ajanta. However, Bagh is recognised as a distinct regional expression rather than simply an exact copy of Ajanta.

Distinguishing Bagh from Ajanta

Ajanta and Bagh share a Buddhist context, a broadly comparable period of artistic development and a tradition of painting on prepared surfaces.

Their strongest identification clues differ:

  • Ajanta: Especially associated with the extensive surviving Jataka narratives, including Shibi and Mahajanaka, and celebrated Bodhisattva paintings.
  • Bagh: Particularly associated with the Rang Mahal and lively depictions of processions, musicians, dancers and courtly life.

These differences are useful identification clues, not absolute exclusions. Ajanta also depicts musicians and courtly settings, and Bagh belongs to a Buddhist cultural environment.

Therefore, a question mentioning dancers alone cannot establish Bagh as the answer. The additional clues of Madhya Pradesh, Dhar district or Rang Mahal make the identification much stronger.

Prelims focus

  • Bagh Caves are located in Dhar district, Madhya Pradesh.
  • They are associated with Buddhism.
  • Their major development occurred around the 4th–6th centuries CE.
  • Bagh originally had 9 caves; 5 are generally described as surviving.
  • Cave 4 is known as Rang Mahal.
  • Important painted subjects include musicians, dancers, processions and courtly life.
  • Trap: Bagh is not in Maharashtra; Ajanta and Ellora are the two Maharashtra sites in this comparison.

[Sources: Government of Madhya Pradesh, Dhar District Administration, 'Bagh Caves', Tourist Places section (consulted 23 November 2026); UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Bagh Cave Paintings', Tentative List reference 7043, 'Description', submitted 8 July 2026 (consulted 23 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: Life around a Buddhist monastery at Bagh.

title: Bagh Caves: Buddhist Murals and Depictions of Courtly Life

body:
Location and historical development

The Ellora Caves, also locally known as Verul Leni, are situated near Aurangabad in Maharashtra.

Ellora is one of India's most important rock-cut architectural complexes. Its principal monuments were developed over several centuries, broadly from the 6th to the 10th centuries CE, with activity at the wider site extending beyond this main period.

Ellora is especially significant because it contains monuments associated with three religious traditions: Buddhism, Hinduism and Jainism.

This makes it different from Ajanta and Bagh, whose principal archaeological and artistic associations are Buddhist.

Religious classification of the caves

The Ellora complex contains 34 principal numbered caves. These are conventionally divided into the following groups:

  • Caves 1–12: Buddhist monuments.
  • Caves 13–29: Hindu or Brahmanical monuments.
  • Caves 30–34: Jain monuments.

The Buddhist caves include monasteries and religious imagery associated with Buddhism. The Hindu group contains major temples and sculptures representing Shaivite and Vaishnavite themes. The Jain caves contain sculptures and paintings associated with Jain religious traditions.

What makes Ellora important for mural painting?

Ellora is particularly famous for its rock-cut architecture and monumental sculpture, but painting was also part of the decoration of its caves.

Fragments of paintings survive in important parts of the complex, including the Hindu Kailasa temple and the Jain caves.

The surviving remains demonstrate that sculpture and painting were not mutually exclusive artistic activities. The same rock-cut religious monument could include carved figures, architectural decoration and painted surfaces.

Cave 16: The Kailasa temple

Cave 16 is the celebrated Kailasa temple, an enormous monolithic rock-cut monument primarily associated with Shiva.

Its construction is traditionally attributed to the Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna I.

The monument is especially important for its architectural achievement and sculptural compositions. A well-known sculptural subject depicts Ravana attempting to shake Mount Kailasa.

Remains of paintings from different periods are also preserved on the ceilings of the front pillared hall of the temple.

The Kailasa temple therefore provides an important example of the relationship between rock-cut sculpture and mural painting.

Cave 32: Indra Sabha

Cave 32, known as Indra Sabha, belongs to the Jain group.

It is associated with elaborate Jain sculpture and surviving painted decoration, including ceiling paintings.

The Jain caves demonstrate that mural painting was not restricted to Buddhism or Hinduism.

Subjects and artistic identification

The religious identity of a particular Ellora cave helps interpret its art:

  • Buddhist caves: Buddhist religious imagery and monastic architecture.
  • Hindu caves: Subjects associated with Shiva, Vishnu and Hindu religious narratives.
  • Jain caves: Jain religious figures, sacred subjects and decorative painting.

Ellora's visual character is strongly marked by monumental carved architecture and sculpture. The surviving mural remains, particularly in later Jain contexts, add evidence of painted religious decoration.

This combination distinguishes Ellora from Ajanta, where extensive surviving Buddhist wall paintings are central to the site's artistic reputation.

Do not confuse sculpture with painting

The famous Ravana-shaking-Kailasa composition at Ellora is a sculptural subject. Its presence in Cave 16 does not make it a mural painting. Ellora contains both sculpture and surviving painted decoration, which should be identified separately.

Comparison with Ajanta

Both Ajanta and Ellora are rock-cut cave complexes in Maharashtra, but their religious range and best-known artistic characteristics differ.

Ajanta is particularly associated with Buddhist narrative murals, including Jataka stories and Bodhisattva figures.

Ellora is associated with Buddhist, Hindu and Jain monuments, outstanding rock-cut sculpture and surviving painted remains in parts of the complex.

The appearance of a Jain cave or the name Indra Sabha is therefore a much stronger clue for Ellora than for Ajanta.

Prelims focus

  • Ellora is located in Maharashtra.
  • It contains 34 principal numbered caves.
  • Caves 1–12 are Buddhist.
  • Caves 13–29 are Hindu.
  • Caves 30–34 are Jain.
  • Cave 16 is the Kailasa temple; Cave 32 is Indra Sabha.
  • Trap: Ellora is not exclusively Buddhist, and it is incorrect to conclude that the complex has no surviving mural paintings.

[Sources: Archaeological Survey of India, 'Ellora Caves', sections describing the historical development and classification of the caves (consulted 23 November 2026); UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Ellora Caves', World Heritage List reference 243, 'Description', including the discussion of Kailasa and the Jain caves (consulted 23 November 2026); NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art Part-I, Class 11, chapter 'Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture', pp. 41–43.]

title: Ellora: Paintings in a Buddhist, Hindu and Jain Cave Complex

body:
Location and historical background

Lepakshi is a historic temple site in Andhra Pradesh, near Hindupur in the region traditionally associated with Anantapur district.

Its most important monument for mural identification is the Veerabhadra Temple, dedicated to a form of Shiva.

The temple is closely associated with the Vijayanagara Empire. Much of its major development belongs to the 16th century CE, particularly the reign of Achyuta Deva Raya.

The temple's development received support from Vijayanagara-period patrons, including Virupanna and Viranna.

The surviving mural paintings provide valuable evidence of the religious narratives, clothing, ornaments and visual conventions of the Vijayanagara period.

Where are the murals found?

The murals occur on the walls and ceilings of the temple's halls and associated spaces.

They are particularly associated with the elaborately decorated mandapas, or pillared halls.

This architectural setting is important for identification. Lepakshi's principal murals belong to a Hindu temple environment rather than the Buddhist monastic cave environment of Ajanta or Bagh.

Principal subjects of Lepakshi painting

The paintings draw upon Hindu religious narratives, Puranic traditions and episodes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata.

Important subjects include:

  • Shiva-related narratives: Different forms of Shiva and events associated with Shaivite traditions.
  • Girija Kalyana: The marriage of Shiva and Parvati.
  • Kiratarjuniya: The story associated with Arjuna's encounter with Shiva appearing as a hunter.
  • Draupadi Swayamvara: An episode associated with the Mahabharata.
  • Ramayana narratives: Episodes associated with Rama and other characters from the epic.

The paintings also represent clothing, jewellery and other aspects of the society in which the temple was decorated.

Although religious stories dominate the murals, these details make them valuable evidence for understanding Vijayanagara-period material culture.

Distinctive features of the Vijayanagara painting style

Lepakshi paintings belong to the mature tradition of Vijayanagara mural art.

A particularly important feature is the treatment of the human face. Figures are frequently shown in profile, with a large or prominently represented eye.

In many figures, the second eye is made visible or emphasised even though the face is shown mainly from the side. This distinctive treatment is an important clue for recognising the Lepakshi style.

The figures and other objects are frequently represented in a relatively flat, two-dimensional manner, rather than with the fuller rounded modelling associated with the mature Ajanta paintings.

Clear outlines establish the shapes of the figures. The compositions are often organised into distinct narrative areas and contain decorative details associated with the temple setting.

These are general characteristics of the Vijayanagara style; individual paintings may vary in their treatment of particular figures and scenes.

How Lepakshi differs from Ajanta

Both Ajanta and Lepakshi contain large narrative paintings, but they belong to different religious and historical settings.

FeatureAjantaLepakshi
StateMaharashtraAndhra Pradesh
Principal settingBuddhist rock-cut cavesHindu temple
Major painting period5th–6th centuries CE16th century CE
Main narrativesJatakas and Buddhist subjectsHindu epics and Puranic subjects
Characteristic figure treatmentRounded modelling and rhythmic linesProfile faces and relatively flat figures

The subject is often the most useful starting point. A Jataka narrative involving King Shibi or Mahajanaka indicates the Buddhist painting tradition of Ajanta. A temple ceiling painting illustrating Kiratarjuniya or Girija Kalyana, combined with the characteristic profile faces, points towards Lepakshi.

Artistic and historical significance

Lepakshi demonstrates that India's mural tradition continued and developed in regional forms long after the major painting activity at Ajanta.

Its paintings also show how Hindu temples served as centres of narrative art. Religious stories were represented through large compositions that could be viewed within the architectural space of the temple.

The visual conventions of Vijayanagara painting influenced later South Indian temple-painting traditions, although those later developments are separate from the core identification of Lepakshi.

Prelims focus

  • Lepakshi is located in Andhra Pradesh, near Hindupur.
  • The important monument is the Veerabhadra Temple.
  • The murals are associated with the Vijayanagara period, especially the 16th century CE.
  • Their subjects include the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Shaivite narratives.
  • Distinctive features include profile faces, prominent eyes and relatively flat figures.
  • Trap: Lepakshi is not an Ajanta-period Buddhist Jataka painting centre; its principal murals belong to a later Hindu temple tradition.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art Part-I, Class 11, chapter 'Later Mural Traditions', p. 65, section 'Vijayanagara Murals'; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Sri Veerabhadra Temple and Monolithic Bull (Nandi), Lepakshi', Tentative List reference 6607, 'Description', submitted 17 February 2022 (consulted 23 November 2026); IIACD, 'Lepakshi Veerabhadraswamy Temple Ceiling Paintings', sections 'History', 'About the Paintings' and 'Aesthetic Elements' (consulted 23 November 2026).]
